title: Walk while you have light (John 12:27–50)
hook: now is my soul troubled; walk while you have the light
tomorrow: he loved them to the end

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Greeks asked to see Jesus, and he talked about a grain of wheat. Your line was unless it dies. What did you let go of? Day six hundred twenty-seven.

Late afternoon light goes gold and long, and there's maybe an hour before dark. Anything you meant to do outside, you'd better do now. Farmers know it. Kids playing in the street know it. Today's passage is the late afternoon of Jesus's public life in John's Gospel. After this, he won't speak to the crowds again. Everything from chapter thirteen on happens in private, with his closest friends, and then on the way to the cross. So these are his last public words. And he begins by admitting something.

"Now is my soul troubled; and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour: but for this cause came I unto this hour." He's troubled, and says so. The other Gospels show it in the garden of Gethsemane; John shows it here. And instead of asking to be spared, he prays: "Father, glorify thy name." Then a voice comes from heaven: "I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again." The crowd hears it differently. Some say it thundered. Others say an angel spoke. The same sound, and people hear what they're ready to hear. Then he says, "And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me." Lifted up: on a cross, and, as John hears it, into glory, both at once. And then comes today's line, with the urgency of sunset: "Yet a little while is the light with you. Walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you." It's not a threat. It's what someone says to a friend when the sun is going down: don't wait. While the light is here, use it. "While ye have light, believe in the light, that ye may be the children of light." Then, John says, he went away and hid himself. Before the curtain falls on the public ministry, Jesus cries out a summary of everything he's said. And it ends gently. He says he came not to judge the world, but to save the world. Some readers call John chapters one to twelve the Book of Signs. Tomorrow, a new part begins.
screen: then, large: `WALK WHILE YE HAVE THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one good thing before dark. Settle, and breathe. Picture today's light. Where is the sun right now? Morning, noon, already going down? Then think of one good thing you've been putting off. A call to an aging parent. An apology. A thank-you note. Visiting someone. Something that won't wait forever. Picture doing it today, while there's still light. Notice any reluctance, and how small it is next to the thing itself. If you pray, you can ask for help to do it. If you don't, simply choose the hour you'll do it. The bell holds the time.
Walk while you have light. Among Jesus's last public words in John: the light is with you a little while longer, so don't wait.

segments.voice: Your line: while you have the light. Today, do the good thing you chose before the sun goes down. Day six hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Christians often read this passage in Holy Week; some pray at sunset, keeping the evening as a time to remember the light while it lasts.

original.note: Greek: walk about, go on your way. Here, how you go through your days.

trapdoor: what you thought: a warning about darkness.
what it means: Jesus's last public words, spoken like a friend at sunset: use the light while it's here.
what a scholar hears: chapter twelve closes what some readers call the Book of Signs, and lifted up points both to the cross and to glory.

notes: 'Book of Signs' (John 1–12) and 'Book of Glory' (13–20/21) are terms associated with C. H. Dodd and Raymond Brown. Confirm 'many scholars'.
Peripatetic derives from Greek peripatein (to walk about), via Aristotle's school. Confirm.
12:44–50 is presented as a summary cry after 12:36b ('departed, and did hide himself'). Confirm.
The double sense of 'lifted up' (hypsoo: crucifixion and exaltation) is standard in commentaries.
